summary:
Amazonas stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America on legal gender recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe, and it is the national picture against which this department is assessed. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one count put hate-crime killings of trans people at 13 in the first quarter of 2025 alone. Sara Millerey, a 32-year trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, and died the following afternoon with no one arrested; her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia, and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation.

Where armed groups operate, the threat is organised and announced. In Caquetá, armed groups gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers against trans women, forcing her to relocate twice after death threats; in Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". An activist quoted in the reporting states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases. Reported totals for that pattern include 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Protection machinery exists alongside that failure. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence against them as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; a Colombian court has also ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising.

No Amazonas-specific finding on law, enforcement practice or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sources available for this entry. The assessment therefore rests on the national framework and the national pattern of violence and prosecution, which apply throughout the country including this department.
tangentialFactors:
The violence documented in the sources is concentrated in two distinct settings, and neither is this department. One is territories under armed-group control, where "social cleansing" campaigns in Caquetá announced through flyers targeted "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" and threatened a further wave, and where trans women reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. The other is ordinary urban settings, where Sara Millerey was attacked in Bello near Medellín and a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April 2025, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands flailing in a creek unable to swim before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was".

Colombia's trajectory is frequently compared with the rest of the region: the notary-based marker change of 2015 and the self-recognition jurisprudence of 1993 place the country ahead of most neighbours on paper, while the murder totals place it among the most dangerous for trans people in practice. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern of conflict-driven violence, and solidarity events were held in several cities after the Millerey killing.
